title: Tenth Strip
context: Grade 4, the first working topic of the decimals chapter. An adult sees a strip being shaded, which squared paper does perfectly well. What is actually being settled is that a tenth is a share of a named whole, and that the two ways of writing it say one amount and not two. A share with no whole behind it is the gap in the reasoning box later in the chapter, where three shares of somebody's spending are handed over and the amount being spent is never named at all.

writeup.why: Cut one whole into ten equal parts, shade some of them, and write what is shaded as a fraction and again with a point.
writeup.look: A long strip lying across the stage with a cutter along it, a naming slot above it and two writing slots beside it.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Tenth Strip' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the shares written against the shares this phase lays out, two numbers in ink, the first climbing by one as each pair of slots fills and the second fixed at however many strips this phase holds. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The naming slot sits across the top left of the working area, 420 by 56 at 64,206, and holds what the whole is: a metre of ribbon, a chapati, a litre of milk. Until something is written in it the cutter stays parked and a tap on the strip springs back with the slot lit and still empty, nothing marked. The strip itself lies under it, 1080 by 150 at 64,274, drawn as one piece with rounded ends. The cutter rides a rail directly beneath it, 1080 by 10 at 64,436, with the count of pieces written above the rail as it is dragged; the strip folds into equal pieces as the cutter travels and settles only on ten, springing back from every other count with the pieces it was holding left lying along the stage. A settled strip shows ten pieces of one length, each 108 wide, touching along their edges so that the whole is still one thing, the dividing lines drawn near-black and no gap opened anywhere between them. A piece is shaded by tapping it and unshaded by tapping again, exactly the number shaded is drawn and no piece overlaps another; shading is amber, because a piece of this strip stands for tenths. Measure the pieces lifts all ten off the strip and stands them end on against a rule, 1080 by 120 at 64,462, where a difference in length is seen rather than argued about, with a small bracket drawn between the longest and the shortest and nothing written in it. The uneven cut control cuts ten pieces of visibly different lengths and asks whether one of the short ones can still be called a tenth, and the same rule measures those. The two writing slots stand along the foot of the working area, the fraction slot 320 by 92 at 200,606 and the slot that takes the point 320 by 92 at 600,606, with a bar 72 by 10 at 528,646 drawn between them that fills only once both are written, because they carry one amount. Inside the slot that takes the point, in front of the point, the ones column is drawn as an open box and stays open until a digit goes into it: a bare point and a digit is handed back with that box lit and the answer left standing exactly as it was entered. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever a share or a single digit is asked for, with a fraction key beside them that draws a bar and opens a box above it and a box below it, and on the first phase a word pad of this strip's own words, whole, equal parts, tenth, tenths, fraction, decimal point and ones place, so that a piece can be named and a slot called with one press. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own: a digit standing to the left of the point is deep blue, a digit standing to the right of it is green, and the point itself is vermilion between them on every phase without exception, because a chapter whose whole subject is one dot cannot afford a frame where the dot has to be hunted for. A part standing for tenths is amber, one standing for hundredths is rose, one standing for thousandths is sky blue, and a zero that is only holding a place open is grey, whether it was written in on the left of a short numerator or printed on the end of a measurement. Chrome never borrows one of those and none of them is ever used for chrome, and every one of the readings survives with the colour taken away, because a place is told by the heading written over it before it is ever told by a colour, a filling zero is told by the short arrow running inward from the point, and a zero printed on the end is told by the place counter that lights it. Grey never means faint: such a zero is drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit and is never dimmed, shrunk or left out. Nothing on this stage ever changes size for emphasis. A shaded piece is drawn the same width as an unshaded one and a piece being talked about is never swollen or shrunk, because on this strip size is carrying the whole of the meaning and a piece that grows to be noticed is a piece that has stopped being a tenth.
writeup.finish: The card shows the strip the child cut, its shaded pieces still coloured, and the fraction and the decimal standing side by side under it.

phases.win: ten pieces of one length settle along the strip and the measure control finds no difference
phases.does: names the whole, runs the cutter, then measures the pieces against one another
phases.goal: one whole cut into ten equal parts gives tenths, and the parts must match
phases.says: Say what you are cutting first. Now cut it into ten. Are the pieces the same?
phases.check: Away from the screen: fold a strip into ten, hand a friend one piece, and tell them what it is one tenth of.
phases.feels: a tenth is a share of something, and the something has to be named before the share says anything
phases.hands: Give each pair a long paper strip and let them fold and cut it into ten pieces without a ruler. Before anything is shaded, ask what the strip is a strip of and write that answer at the top of the sheet. Then stack the ten pieces and look at the edges. Cut a second strip with a ruler and stack those. Ask which of the two strips a tenth can be taken from, and what the other one would be describing if a share were written down from it.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: how many pieces is this strip cut into? Second rung, the phase's: are they all the same size? Third rung: the strip is cut to two pieces with one plainly longer than the other and the child says whether either of them is a half. The word pad stays open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: ten is the number the rule asks for and a count is easy to check, while lengths are not, so a strip with the right number of pieces looks like a strip that was cut right.
wrong.move: cuts the strip into ten pieces by eye, counts ten of them, and calls any one of them a tenth.
wrong.screen: the ten pieces lift off the strip and stand end on against the rule in the order they were cut, and the two that overhang the rest are left standing there with the bracket drawn between the longest and the shortest. The child's strip is left exactly as it was cut, a second strip is cut by the cutter beside it and measured the same way, and both sets of pieces stay standing on the rule together with nothing marked.

wrong.why: a picture with part of it coloured in looks like a question that has already been asked, and the strip is the only thing on the stage to count.
wrong.move: shades some pieces and writes the share down while the naming slot above the strip is still empty.
wrong.screen: both writing slots hand the answer back and stay empty, with the naming slot lit above the strip and the shaded pieces left exactly as the child shaded them. The voice then asks the question the reasoning box later in the chapter never asks, which is one tenth of what, and the slots stay shut until the strip has been called a ribbon, a chapati or a litre of milk.

phases.screen: an uncut strip with an empty naming slot above it and the cutter waiting
phases.soWhat: One whole cut into ten equal parts gives tenths, and the parts have to be the same size or none of them is a tenth.
phases.concept: Splitting one into ten equal parts

phases.win: both slots fill and a bar is drawn joining them, because they carry one amount
phases.does: writes the shaded amount in the fraction slot and then in the decimal slot
phases.goal: a share is written over ten and with a point, and the two carry one amount
phases.says: Write it over ten. Now write the very same thing with a point.
phases.check: Write four tenths of a ribbon in two different ways, and then say which of the two is the larger amount.
phases.feels: two ways of writing it down, one strip, and the same pieces coloured under both of them
phases.hands: Take a strip already cut into ten and shade four pieces. Write the amount over ten on one line of the page and with a point on the line under it, and draw a line joining the two. Then cover one of the two lines with a hand and let a partner shade a fresh strip from the other. Do it again with six pieces, and ask whether the second line ever had to be worked out or only written.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many pieces are shaded? Second rung, the phase's: which of the two slots is still waiting? Third rung: the strip is cut to two pieces with one of them shaded and the child fills both slots from it. The number pad and the fraction key stay open.

wrong.why: one right answer to a question that asked for one amount feels like the whole job, and the second slot reads as the same thing being asked twice over.
wrong.move: writes the fraction, leaves the slot that takes the point empty, and reports the strip finished.
wrong.screen: both slots stay on the stage with the child's fraction standing exactly where it was written and the second slot still empty, and the joining bar is drawn as a faint outline waiting to fill. The strip is read out again with the shaded pieces lighting one at a time, and the same count is asked for in the other slot with nothing cleared.

wrong.why: the two forms look nothing like each other on the line, and every other pair of different-looking numbers met so far has been a pair of different numbers.
wrong.move: takes four tenths and the decimal for it to be two different sizes, because one is written with two numbers and the other with one.
wrong.screen: the two written forms are carried down to the strip together and laid under the very same four shaded pieces, neither of them shading anything more or anything less. The joining bar fills between them, and a second strip is drawn under the first and shaded to the child's other reading, which asks for pieces this strip does not have; both strips are left standing.

phases.screen: the cut strip with some pieces shaded and both writing slots empty
phases.soWhat: A share is written as a fraction over ten and also with a decimal point, and the two say the same amount.
phases.concept: The same amount, written with a point

phases.win: the digit lands and the shaded pieces light one at a time as it is counted back
phases.does: counts the shaded pieces and writes the digit that goes after the point
phases.goal: the digit after the point counts how many tenths there are
phases.says: How many tenths are shaded? That is the digit after the point.
phases.check: A strip of ten has six pieces shaded. Write the decimal, and say what the six is counting.
phases.feels: the digit after the point is a count of pieces, and nothing else on the line moves when it changes
phases.hands: Shade seven pieces of a ten piece strip and write the decimal. Then shade nine on a second strip and write that one. Put the two written numbers one under the other and ask what changed between them and what did not, and insist the answer is said as a sentence about the digit after the point rather than about the number as a whole.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which pieces are you counting, the shaded ones or the plain ones? Second rung, the phase's: which column does that count get written in? Third rung: the strip is cut to two pieces with the tenths column labelled over the slot and the child counts and writes. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: the shaded count and the number of pieces are the two facts the strip hands over, and a decimal looks like somewhere that both of them could go.
wrong.move: puts both of the fraction's numbers on the line, writing seven point one zero for seven pieces of ten.
wrong.screen: the number the child wrote is carried to a fresh strip and read off it place by place. The seven lands in the ones column as seven whole strips, and seven whole strips are drawn out along the stage beside the single strip that was shaded. Both stand together, nothing is cleared, and the shaded strip is then read back with the count of pieces spoken into the tenths place on its own.

wrong.why: on a strip with a few pieces coloured the plain pieces are the bigger picture, and the question does not say out loud which of the two runs it is asking about.
wrong.move: counts the pieces that are not shaded, because the plain run of them is the longer one.
wrong.screen: the shaded pieces light one at a time from the left with the count written above them as it climbs, and the plain run is left plain and uncounted. The child's digit stays in the slot, a copy of the strip is drawn underneath with the child's count shaded instead, and the two strips stand together with plainly different amounts coloured in.

phases.screen: a strip with several pieces shaded and the decimal slot waiting
phases.soWhat: The digit after the point counts how many tenths there are.

phases.win: the zero settles in the ones column and the column lights to show it is empty of whole ones
phases.does: adds the zero, then reads the number aloud with the ones column lit
phases.goal: the zero before the point holds the ones place open
phases.says: Something is missing in front of the point. What is it holding?
phases.check: Away from the screen: write four tenths of a kilogram properly on a label, and say what the zero you wrote is holding.
phases.feels: the zero is not filling a gap, it is holding a column open where there are no whole ones
phases.hands: Write a price on a scrap of paper as a bare point and a five, hand it across the room, and ask for it to be read out. Then write the same thing again with the zero in front and hand that over. Ask which of the two was easier to read and what the zero is actually saying about whole rupees. Finish by writing four tenths of a kilogram on a label for the class cupboard.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which column stands in front of the point? Second rung, the phase's: how many whole ones does this number have? Third rung: the strip is put away and a two column chart headed ones and tenths takes its place, and the child fills both columns. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: nothing is being counted there, and a column with nothing in it looks like a column that does not need anything written in it at all.
wrong.move: leaves the ones place empty, because there are no whole ones to write in it.
wrong.screen: the ones column stays drawn as an open box in front of the point and stays open, with the child's bare point and digit left exactly as they were entered. The number is then read out from that column rightwards, the reading stops on the open box, and the voice names the column the box belongs to. A grey zero is offered from the tray and the same reading is run again with it in place.

wrong.why: in front of was heard as make space in front, and making space for something usually means shifting whatever is already standing there.
wrong.move: writes the zero in and slides the digit along to make room, turning five tenths into five hundredths.
wrong.screen: both readings are carried down to strips. Five pieces of ten are shaded under the first, and under the second the whole is cut into a hundred and five of those cells are shaded, so the two pictures stand side by side and are plainly ten times apart. The child's number stays exactly where it was written, and the grey zero is then walked into the ones column with the five held still in the tenths place the whole way.

phases.screen: a decimal written into the slot as a bare point and a digit, with nothing in front of it
phases.soWhat: The zero before the point holds the ones place open and says there are no whole ones.
phases.concept: What the zero in front is for

writeup.delight: The first phase, the moment the measure is run on a strip that was cut by eye. The ten pieces lift off the strip together and stand themselves end on against the rule along the foot, in the order they were cut and not sorted, so the two that overhang the rest are plainly out of line; the bracket is drawn between the longest and the shortest with nothing written in it. Run the same measure on a strip the cutter settled, and the ten stand level, the bracket closes to nothing and the strip re-forms itself into one piece with the pieces sliding back into place. Both runs can be made as often as a finger likes, nothing is marked either way, and the voice says nothing at all while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase an uncut strip lies along the ledge with the naming slot above it standing empty and the cutter parked at its left hand end. On the second the strip is already cut into ten with four pieces shaded, and the two writing slots stand along the foot of the working area with the joining bar between them drawn as a faint outline. On the third a strip stands with seven pieces shaded and the fraction slot already filled, so only the slot that takes the point is waiting. On the fourth a decimal sits in the slot as a bare point and a digit, with the ones column in front of it drawn as an open box and nothing in it. The running count at the top left holds the shares written against the shares this phase lays out, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the empty naming slot, or the joining bar, or the leftmost shaded piece, or the open ones column, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks what the strip is a strip of. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any whole, any number of shaded pieces, with both writing slots and the uneven cut control open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on cutting one whole into ten equal parts, writing a share two ways, counting tenths, and the zero that holds the ones place.
voiceLines: A long strip, and nothing cut yet. Say what it is before the cutter runs.
Say what you are cutting first. Now cut it into ten. Are the pieces the same?
Write it over ten. Now write the very same thing with a point.
How many tenths are shaded? That is the digit after the point.
Something is missing in front of the point. What is it holding?
Another whole. Name it first, then cut it into ten.
Free play. Any whole, any pieces shaded, both writing slots and the uneven cut open.
Stand the pieces against one another, then count the shaded ones again.
Every share written twice over, and the zero standing in the ones place each time.

observations.why: A share is a share of something, and until the something is named there is nothing for it to be a share of.
observations.soWhat: Two tenths of nobody's money is not an amount, and asking of what is the first move, not a quibble.
observations.observe: The slots would not take a share until the strip above them had been given a name.

observations.why: Tenths are ten equal parts of one whole, and the word equal is doing work in that sentence.
observations.soWhat: Counting ten pieces is not enough; they have to be the same size or none of them is a tenth.
observations.observe: Ten pieces cut by eye stood at different heights on the rule, and ten cut properly stood level.

observations.why: Both are ways of writing how much of the strip is coloured, and the colouring did not change between them.
observations.soWhat: A fraction over ten and a decimal with one place are one amount written two ways.
observations.observe: The fraction and the decimal were written from the very same shaded pieces and the bar joined them.

observations.why: The column is there whether or not any whole ones are being counted, and a zero is how you say there are none.
observations.soWhat: The zero before the point is holding a column open, which is not the same as filling a gap.
observations.observe: The ones column in front of the point stayed drawn and open until something was put in it.

source_tool.description: A long strip lies across the stage with a cutter running along it. The child names the whole first: a metre of ribbon, a chapati, a litre of milk. Nothing can be cut until the whole has a name, and a share asked for before the whole is named is handed back with the naming slot lit and empty. The cutter then folds the strip into equal pieces and settles only on ten: a strip left at seven or at twelve springs back, and the pieces are laid against one another along the stage so the difference can be seen rather than argued about. Pieces are shaded by tapping and unshaded by tapping again. Two writing slots stand beside the strip, one taking the amount written over ten and one taking the same amount written with a point, and both have to be filled before the strip is finished, so the two forms are always written together rather than one instead of the other. A zero guard watches the decimal slot: an answer entered as a bare point and a digit is handed back with the empty ones column lit in front of it. An uneven cut control cuts ten pieces that are plainly not the same size and asks whether one of them can still be called a tenth.
source_tool.art_direction: A ribbon strip on a cutting ledge / Picture book

wrong.note: A soft low double-bloop. A nudge, never a buzzer.

modes.freePlay: Out of scope here. It is not reached from inside a phase mount, because a phase mount ends idle and has no finish card to reach it from. writeup.freePlay stays as the record of what that activity is, for whoever builds it as its own thing.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: a strip that can be cut, a ten by ten grid whose cells can be tapped, digit cards that can be picked up, a point card of its own, a ruled place chart with a heading over every column, a kitchen scale with a printing display, and a balance beam.

A whole is always drawn split into parts of the same size, with the parts touching so that the whole is still one thing. Exactly the stated number of parts is drawn, exactly the stated number of them is shaded, and no part overlaps another.

A decimal is always drawn with its point standing clearly between the two parts and never floating above or below the line. Where the two parts are named, the whole number part is named on the left and the decimal part on the right.

A place chart always carries a named heading over every column, holds one digit to a column, and keeps a column of its own for the dot between the ones and the tenths. A bare row of digits with no chart behind it is never used to teach place value.

A zero filling an empty decimal place is drawn arriving from the point outwards, on the left of the digits already there, with a short arrow running inward from the point. That arrow never runs the other way.

A zero printed on the end of a decimal is drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit, and it is never dimmed, shrunk, tidied away or quietly dropped. The whole teaching of the closing topic is that it counts.

Two answers being compared stand on the stage at the same time, one above the other, with whatever measures the difference between them drawn in between. An answer that has been replaced is never cleared away.
A column, a place or a part is told apart by its label first and by its colour second, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a digit, a part or a card the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. These are the chapter's own colours, so a tool and a picture of the same thing are the same colour. A digit to the left of the point is deep blue and a digit to the right of it is green, with the decimal point itself vermilion between them in every tool without exception, because a chapter whose whole subject is one dot cannot afford a frame where the dot has to be hunted for. A part standing for tenths is amber, one standing for hundredths is rose and one standing for thousandths is sky blue, and those three hold from the strip to the grid to the chart. A zero holding a place open is grey, whether it was filled in on the left of a short numerator or printed on the end of a measurement, because it is the one digit here doing a job rather than counting something. Grey never means faint: such a zero is drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit and is never dimmed, shrunk or left out. All of that holds in greyscale, because a filling zero is told apart by the short arrow running inward from the point, and a printed zero on the end by the place counter that lights it.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Stand the pieces against one another, then count the shaded ones again.
voice.onNext: Another whole. Name it first, then cut it into ten.
voice.opening: A long strip, and nothing cut yet. Say what it is before the cutter runs.
voice.onFinish: Every share written twice over, and the zero standing in the ones place each time.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Any whole, any pieces shaded, both writing slots and the uneven cut open.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

placement.where: Straight after a paper strip has been folded and cut into ten by hand, and before anything has been written down. The tool is what refuses to let a share be named before the whole is, which paper cannot refuse.

answer_key.rule: One whole cut into ten equal parts gives tenths, and the parts have to be the same size or none of them is a tenth. A share is written as a fraction over ten and also with a decimal point, and the two say the same amount. The digit after the point counts how many tenths. The zero before the point holds the ones place and says there are no whole ones, and it is written every time. A share of something is not an amount until the something has been named.
answer_key.wrong: The strip is laid out again and its ten pieces are measured against one another along the stage, then the shaded pieces are counted aloud into both slots in turn. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: The strip is one whole and it has been cut into ten equal pieces, so each piece is one tenth.
Six pieces are coloured, so the coloured part is six out of ten, written 6/10.
A fraction with ten underneath is written with one digit after the point, so 6/10 is 0.6.
items.question: A paper strip is cut into ten equal pieces and six of them are coloured. Write the coloured part as a fraction and as a decimal.
items.checkpoint: Ten equal parts of one whole are tenths, and the pieces have to be the same size.
items.misconception: Counting ten pieces that are not the same size and still calling one of them a tenth.

steps: Ten equal lengths means each one is one tenth of the whole ribbon.
Four of them are used, so the part used is four tenths, written 4/10.
Written with a point that is 0.4, and the dot standing between the zero and the four is the decimal point.
items.answer: 4/10, written 0.4, and the dot is called the decimal point
items.question: A ribbon is cut into ten equal lengths and four of the lengths are used. Write the part used as a fraction and with a point, and name the dot.
items.checkpoint: The fraction and the decimal are two ways of writing one amount, not two amounts.
items.misconception: Treating 4/10 and 0.4 as two different sizes because they look different on the line.

steps: Ten equal beds means one bed is one tenth of the whole garden.
Seven beds are planted, so seven tenths of the garden is planted.
Seven tenths is written 0.7, and the seven sits in the tenths place, counting tenths.
items.answer: 0.7, and the digit after the point counts tenths
items.question: A garden is divided into ten equal beds and seven of the beds are planted. Write the planted part as a decimal, and say what the digit after the point counts.
items.checkpoint: The digit after the point says how many tenths, and nothing else about the writing changes.
items.misconception: Writing seven tenths as 7.10 or as 10.7 by putting both numbers on the line.

steps: The ones column in front of the point has been left with nothing written in it at all.
A zero goes there to say that there are no whole ones, which is not the same as saying nothing.
It also stops the point being missed when the sign is read quickly, so the proper form is 0.6.
items.answer: The zero in front of the point is missing, so the sign should read 0.6
items.question: A shop sign is written as a bare point and a six, with nothing in front of the point. What is missing, and why does it matter?
items.checkpoint: The zero before the point holds the ones place and says there are no whole ones.
items.misconception: Leaving the ones place blank because nothing is there, and losing the point along with it.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: A strip is cut into ten equal pieces and three of them are shaded. Write the shaded part as a decimal.
A child folds a strip into ten pieces, but two of the pieces come out much longer than the rest. Can one of the short pieces be called one tenth?
items.final_answer: No, because tenths are ten equal parts, so every piece has to be the same size

items.question: A one litre bottle is marked in ten equal steps and the milk stands at the eighth mark. Write that amount with a point.
In 0.7, which part is the decimal point, and what does the seven count?
items.final_answer: The dot standing between the zero and the seven is the decimal point, and the seven counts seven tenths

items.question: Five of the ten equal parts of a chapati are eaten. Write the part that was eaten as a decimal.
A strip of ten equal pieces has nine of them shaded. Write the shaded part and the unshaded part as decimals.
items.final_answer: 0.9 is shaded and 0.1 is not, and the two together rebuild one whole

items.question: A friend says they spent two tenths of their pocket money on a pen. How many rupees did the pen cost?
items.final_answer: It cannot be said yet, because nobody has said how much the pocket money was; two tenths is a share until the amount is named

items.question: A sign reads as a bare point and a four, with a kilogram after it. Write it properly, and say what the zero you added is doing.
items.final_answer: 0.4 kg, and the zero holds the ones place to show there are no whole kilograms

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: asks what is being cut before the cutter will run
folds the strip into equal pieces and settles only on ten
lays the pieces against one another to show whether they match
colours a piece by tapping it and uncolours it by tapping again
takes the shaded amount written over ten
takes the same amount written with a point
lights the empty ones column when the decimal is written without it
cuts ten pieces that are not the same size and asks whether one is a tenth

teaching_notes: Cut a real strip before the tool is opened, and cut one badly on purpose. A strip folded into ten pieces that are not the same size is the quickest way to settle what the word equal is doing in the rule, and it takes a minute. Then use the tool for the thing paper will not do: it refuses to cut anything until the child has said what is being cut. Keep that habit, because the reasoning box later in the chapter hands over three shares of somebody's spending and never says one tenth of what. The only amount printed beside them is a bank balance, which is what is left rather than what is being shared out, so a child who reaches for it is being led somewhere the question does not intend. Ask the class what is missing before anybody starts working, and let them find that it is simply not there. Insist on both writing slots every time. A child who writes only the fraction, or only the decimal, has learnt one form and not the tie between them, and the rest of the chapter is that tie run in both directions. Finish on the zero in front of the point, and say what it is holding rather than that it must be written. A child who writes it as a rule will drop it the first time they are hurrying.
generation_prompt: Build a splitting tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A long horizontal strip lies across the working area with a naming slot above it and a cutter running along its length. The naming slot has to be filled before the cutter will run, and a shade attempted on an unnamed strip springs back with the naming slot lit and still empty. The cutter folds the strip into equal pieces and settles only on ten; a strip left at any other count springs back and its pieces are laid against one another along the stage so the difference can be seen. Pieces are shaded by tapping and unshaded by tapping again, exactly the shaded number is drawn, and no piece overlaps another. Two writing slots stand down the right of the canvas, one taking the amount written over ten and one taking the same amount written with a point, and a bar is drawn joining them once both are filled. A zero guard watches the decimal slot: an answer entered as a bare point and a digit is handed back with the empty ones column lit in front of the point, with nothing marked. An uneven cut control cuts the strip into ten pieces of visibly different lengths and asks whether one of them can be called a tenth, measuring them against one another once the answer lands. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Say what you are cutting before you cut it. Cut the whole into ten equal pieces. Shade the pieces you want. Write the shaded amount over ten, then write it again with a point. Put the zero in front of the point every time.
